Volume 10 · Chapter 11

Incomplete markets and advanced derivatives

Graduate Author-reviewed · Prerequisites: v10-c10

By the endExplain why some contingent claims cannot be uniquely priced by replication.

Volume 10 · Chapter 11

Incomplete markets and advanced derivatives

After this chapter, you should be able to exhibit two arbitrage-free prices for the same unspanned claim, compute exact stock-and-cash hedge bounds, identify the exposure that a delta hedge leaves behind, and translate an exotic or credit contract into dated, history-dependent cash flows. A numerical price is an implication of a market, a contract and a choice of valuation rule. More decimal places cannot supply a missing hedging instrument.

Prerequisites. Use the finite replication and positive state prices of Chapter 6, the localized stochastic integrals and scalar Itô formula of Chapter 7, the explicitly proved constant normal-density tilt of Chapter 8, and the sensitivity and error distinctions of Chapter 9 and Chapter 10. This chapter proves its additional finite-state optimization, independent-driver calculus and scheduled finite-jump identities. General stochastic Girsanov, martingale representation, Lévy calculus and Heston existence or transform formulas are not assumed.

1. What an incomplete market leaves undetermined

Fix dates 0 and T and n states, each with strictly positive physical probability Pi. A default-free bank investment of one currency unit pays R=1/D>0 at T; D is the date-0 discount factor. A non-dividend-paying stock costs S0 and pays xi in state i. Short positions and borrowing are unrestricted; there are no transaction costs. Stock trading occurs only at 0 and T. A portfolio with Δ shares and terminal bank cash A costs ΔS0+DA and pays Δxi+A. Completeness means that every vector of state payoffs is attainable by the permitted strategies. With only these two independent securities and more than two states, most vectors are not.

A positive pricing probability vector p satisfies pi>0, Σpi=1 and Σpixi=F, where F=S0/D. Its state prices are πi=Dpi. For every stock-and-cash portfolio, cost=Σπipayoffi. Therefore a nonnegative payoff with a positive component cannot have nonpositive cost. This proves absence of arbitrage directly, including an initially negative-cost portfolio after investing its receipts in the bank. We use strictly positive probabilities because every listed state is physically possible. A physical probability vector need not satisfy the pricing restriction; changing its positive weights does not change these attainable payoffs or arbitrage inequalities.

If an additional terminal claim h is quoted at c=DΣpihi, the same positive state prices also price any portfolio including that claim; hence the enlarged date-0/T market has no arbitrage. This is a sufficient construction, not an assumption that every statistical probability is risk-neutral. Haugh’s finite-market notes provide a broader treatment. Our bounds below are proved without importing a general linear-programming duality theorem.

Worked example 1: three states and a genuinely open price interval

Let S0=100, R=26/25=1.04 and x=(60,100,140). A strike-100 call pays h=(0,0,40). Solving Σp=1 and Σpx=104 gives

p=(a, 9/10−2a, 1/10+a),   0<a<9/20;
c(a)=(25/26)(4+40a),   50/13<c<275/13.

At a=1/5, p=(1/5,1/2,3/10) and c=150/13≈11.538462. The payoff is not affine in x: a line through its first two zeros would also be zero at 140. The subhedge x−100 costs 50/13≈3.846154 and pays (−40,0,40). The superhedge x/2−30 costs 275/13≈21.153846 and pays (0,20,40). At the lower quote, buy the call and short its subhedge: zero initial cost, terminal payoff (40,0,0). At the upper quote, buy the superhedge and short the call: payoff (0,20,0). Both are arbitrages because the relevant states have positive physical probability. Thus the endpoints are limiting bounds, not admissible quotes for this unspanned claim. Above or below the interval the same trades also provide a positive initial receipt.

By contrast, h=x−100 is replicable and its sole no-arbitrage price 50/13 is included. An example physical law (1/2,2/5,1/10) has EPx=84, not 104. Discounting its call expectation would quote 50/13, precisely the excluded lower endpoint; a forecast does not select a risk-neutral measure.

2. Exact hedge bounds, with a constructive proof

Assume min x<F<max x. Allow repeated stock outcomes: distinct histories can have the same terminal stock price. Define the closed set K={p≥0:Σp=1,Σpx=F}. Its boundary includes laws that assign zero weight to possible states. For any h define

L=sup{ΔS0+DA : A+Δxi≤hi for every i},
U=inf{ΔS0+DA : A+Δxi≥hi for every i}.

Every p∈K gives L≤DΣpihi≤U by taking expectations of the hedge inequalities. To prove equality and compute the extrema, two elementary observations suffice.

First, expectations attain extrema on supports of size at most two. K is a closed bounded nonempty subset of finite-dimensional space, so a linear expectation has a maximizer and minimizer. If a feasible p has at least three positive coordinates, find a nonzero vector z supported there with Σz=Σzx=0: these are two homogeneous equations in at least three unknowns. If Σzh≠0, move p slightly in the improving sign, contradicting extremality; if Σzh=0, move without changing value until a coordinate first becomes zero. The move has finite length because z has both positive and negative coordinates. Repeating leaves at most two coordinates. For a pair i,j with xi≠xj, the weights are (xj−F)/(xj−xi) and its complement, retained only when both are nonnegative. A singleton is feasible only if xi=F. A pair with equal x=F reduces to singletons. The same reduction, splitting in both directions and expressing the original point as their convex combination, proves that these listed laws generate all of K.

Second, optimizing a line attains the matching bound. For fixed slope Δ, the cheapest superhedge has intercept maxi(hi−Δxi). Its cost divided by D is

g(Δ)=ΔF+maxi(hi−Δxi).

This continuous piecewise affine function goes to +∞ in both directions: use the minimum-x state for Δ→+∞ and the maximum-x state for Δ→−∞. It has a minimum, which can be chosen at a breakpoint, even if an entire intervening interval is flat. At a minimum, the slopes F−xi of the active lines must straddle zero; if they were all positive or all negative a small move would lower g. Consequently two binding states bracket F, or a binding state has x=F. Their feasible weights produce Eph=A+ΔF exactly. Thus U=D maxKEph. Applying the same argument to −h gives L=D minKEph. Every needed breakpoint is the intersection of two lines with distinct x, so enumeration of their affine stock hedges is sufficient. Repeated x values retain separate payoff inequalities; never merge different histories merely because the stock prices coincide.

Why positivity removes the endpoints. The average of all the listed one- and two-state laws is strictly positive. Indeed every state with x<F can be paired with a state above F, every state above F with one below, and a state at F has its singleton. Call that average p0. If h is not replicable, every attained subhedge has some strict shortfall and every attained superhedge has some strict excess. Their expectations under any strictly positive p give L<DEph<U. Conversely, for any c strictly between L and U, mix a sufficiently small positive amount of p0 with a convex combination of a minimizing and maximizing law to obtain a strictly positive law pricing h at c. If L=U, a superhedge and subhedge must both equal h component by component: their nonnegative gaps have zero expectation under p0. Hence h is affine in x and is replicable. We have proved the full date-0/T price set: the singleton {L} if replicable, and the open interval (L,U) otherwise.

Deleting a physically impossible state changes the market and its bounds. Trading constraints, intermediate solvency requirements, bid–ask quotes and transaction costs also change the optimization. Here a hedge may borrow at intermediate cash-flow dates; the stated bounds guarantee terminal accumulated wealth, not a separate liquidity buffer at every date. Negative rates are permitted because only D>0 was used.

3. The small extension of Itô calculus that we need

Let W1,W2 be independent Brownian motions relative to their joint completed Brownian filtration. Joint future increments are independent of its past. Existence of this probability space is taken from the Brownian construction prerequisite. For a deterministic partition of [0,t] with mesh tending to zero,

E[(Σ ΔW1,iΔW2,i)²]=Σ(Δti)²≤t·mesh→0.

Cross terms vanish by independence and zero means. With bounded adapted weights Hi known at the left endpoints, the corresponding sum still has mean zero and second moment at most ||H||2∞Σ(Δt)2, by conditioning successive increments on the past. Thus weighted cross variation is zero. The same-driver weighted centered-square sum has second moment at most 2||H||2∞Σ(Δt)2. Isometry, conditioning and approximation by elementary predictable processes also give E[(∫u dW1)(∫v dW2)]=0 for square-integrable adapted integrands; u and v need not themselves be independent.

For continuous adapted coefficients, put dXa=badt+Σk=1,2σakdWk, a=1,2. Stop on compact sets that bound X, b, σ and the derivatives of f. For f continuously differentiable in time and twice continuously differentiable in the two spatial variables, all these derivatives jointly continuous, we claim

df=ftdt+ΣafadXa+½Σa,bfab(Σkσakσbk)dt.

Proof of the extension. On a partition, freeze each σ at the left endpoint. If ei is the vector of errors in replacing its two stochastic increments, isometry and (u+v)²≤2u²+2v² give EΣ||ei||²≤2Σa,kE∫|σak(s)−σak(ti)|²ds→0 by boundedness and pathwise continuity. The frozen squared increments have bounded expected sum. Cauchy–Schwarz therefore makes every error product vanish in probability. Drift squares and drift–diffusion products vanish by the same bound and Σ(Δt)²→0. The weighted diagonal and cross Brownian estimates above leave exactly Σσakσbkdt. The first-order sums converge to the ordinary and Itô integrals by continuity and isometry. A time increment can be separated before the spatial increment; uniform continuity of ft controls its error by t times a vanishing modulus. The spatial Taylor remainder is bounded by a vanishing modulus of the maximum increment times Σ||ΔX||², which is bounded in probability. This proves the identity up to the compact stop. A stopped coefficient has a possible discontinuity at the stopping time; bounded dominated convergence still gives the freezing estimate because a single time has zero Lebesgue measure. Increase the compact sets to obtain the formula before explosion or exit from the declared open state domain. Random initial values are covered by the same localization. For a terminally nonsmooth payoff apply the result only through U<T, with any terminal limit justified separately.

In particular [W1,W2]t=0. If Wv=ρW1+√(1−ρ²)W2, |ρ|≤1, its Gaussian independent increments have variance Δt, so it is Brownian and [W1,Wv]t=ρt. No general characterization of Brownian local martingales is needed.

4. Stochastic volatility: identify the unspanned exposure

Consider an existing continuous adapted solution, before its exit from an open domain, to

dS=μSdt+σ(Y)S dW1,
dY=b dt+β[ρdW1+√(1−ρ²)dW2].

S>0, σ(Y)>0; b and β may be continuous adapted coefficients. Y is a volatility factor, not necessarily the variance itself. Existence and positivity for an arbitrary proposed factor SDE are additional obligations, not consequences of this notation. For a smooth candidate claim value V(t,S,Y), the two random coefficients from the proved formula are

dW1: σS VS+ρβVY;   dW2: β√(1−ρ²)VY.

A funded stock-and-bank strategy has only the first Brownian coefficient, ΔσS. Bank interest and proportional stock dividends are finite-variation cash flows, so neither spans the second driver. When β√(1−ρ²)VY≠0 over a positive amount of time, exact matching is impossible. More formally, equality of two continuous semimartingales forces the quadratic variation of their difference to vanish; the second-driver contribution is the integral of this nonnegative squared coefficient. The best instantaneous variance match uses Δ=VS+ρβVY/(σS), leaving instantaneous variance β²(1−ρ²)VY². This is a local exposure result, not a globally optimal hedge under arbitrary costs or preferences.

Worked example 2: a second risk factor and a second instrument

At one state take S=100, σ=.20, β=.30, ρ=−.60, VS=.55 and VY=12. The claim’s random coefficients are 20(.55)−.18(12)=8.84 and .24(12)=2.88 currency units per square root of a year. Holding .442 shares removes the first; local residual variance is 2.88²dt=8.2944dt. Holding only the partial delta .55 leaves coefficients −2.16 and 2.88, variance 12.96dt. Quoted vega with respect to a fixed Black–Scholes input is not automatically VY; a specified mapping is required.

Suppose another traded smooth claim G has GS=.25 and GY=6 at this state. Take η=VY/GY=2 units of G and Δ=VS−ηGS=.05 shares, financing the residual value in the bank. Both random coefficients now match. The local exposure determinant is σS·β√(1−ρ²)GY=28.8, so the two equations are invertible. This does not prove that a global hedge exists, remains integrable, survives a zero of GY, or is feasible with discrete trading. If |ρ|=1 or β=0 the orthogonal exposure vanishes; merely counting named factors would then misdiagnose the local rank.

A concrete family of valuation measures, without general Girsanov. To establish that the missing price is real, set r=q=0, Y=W2, and σ(y)=.20+.05 tanh(y). Define

St=S0exp{∫0tσ(Yu)dW1,u−½∫0tσ(Yu)²du}.

Scalar Itô gives dS=σ(Y)S dW1 and S>0. The integrand is continuous and bounded between .15 and .25. On [0,T], define dQλ/dP=exp(−λW2,T−λ²T/2) for any real constant λ. The Gaussian completion-of-the-square proof from Chapter 8 applies to the second coordinate; the first coordinate’s density factor is unchanged. Factoring the joint increment density shows that W1 and B2=W2+λt remain independent Brownian motions relative to the joint filtration under Qλ. Positivity and normalization give equivalence. Thus dY=−λdt+dB2, while the stock still has zero drift and volatility σ(Y). Stochastic-integral identities transfer between these equivalent finite-horizon laws because convergence in probability is preserved by absolute continuity.

Here zero drift really gives a true martingale. Stop S at levels m and 1/m. Itô applied to S² and expectation yield E St∧τm²≤S0²+.25²∫0tE Su∧τm²du, hence ≤S0²e.25²t. The integral inequality follows by iterating its integral operator: its k-th remainder is bounded by a constant times (Ct)k/k!, which tends to zero. The explicit continuous positive exponential has finite maximum and positive minimum on a compact horizon, so τm→T, and Fatou gives the same bound for E St². Therefore E∫σ²S²dt<∞ and the stock integral is a true L² martingale. The argument works under every Qλ.

The bounded factor digital H=1{YT>0} has price EQλH=Φ(−λ√T). At T=1, λ=0 gives .5; λ=1 gives approximately .158655254. Both positive measures price the same bank and stock. In the class of strategies whose gains are true square-integrable martingales under the two laws, replication would require a single initial cost equal to both expectations, a contradiction. Each proposed digital price can itself be extended using its conditional-expectation price process; its bounded martingale and the stock admit the same no-arbitrage expectation argument for admissible gains. We have proved a particular stochastic-volatility incompleteness example, not a universal Heston theorem.

If one selects a Markov factor drift bQ and smooth coefficients under a pricing law, a candidate smooth value can be verified by applying our formula to e−rtV. Its drift is zero when

Vt+(r−q)S VS+bQVY+½σ²S²VSS+ρσSβVSY+½β²VYY−rV=0.

To conclude V=EQ[discounted payoff], one still needs the terminal condition and a true-martingale or uniform-integrability limit, as in Chapter 8. We have not proved PDE existence, uniqueness for arbitrary growth, or that every bQ defines an equivalent measure. The explicit family above proves freedom in one bounded example. In general the chosen factor risk premium needs prices of additional claims, preferences or other assumptions. Fitting a finite set of vanilla quotes constrains parameters within a selected family; it does not prove that family or identify every joint path law. Haugh’s extension notes are a route to stochastic-volatility and jump models; their broader measure-change and transform results require further theory.

5. A jump cannot be crossed by continuous delta rebalancing

For a modest, fully specified extension, let 0<u1<…<um≤T be deterministic event dates. Between dates S follows a continuous diffusion with continuous adapted coefficients, and at uj it changes by an adapted random amount Jj, possibly zero. Suppose the continuous pieces and their left limits exist without explosion. For f∈C1,2, localize on compacts inside its domain. Apply the scalar formula on each continuous interval, take its endpoint limit, add the exact change f(uj,Su_j)−f(uj,Su_j−), and telescope. Finite sums and bounded localization justify all endpoint limits. This proves

f(t,St)−f(0,S0)=∫ftdu+∫fSdSc+½∫fSSb²du
+Σu_j≤t[f(uj,Su_j)−f(uj,Su_j−)],

where b is the continuous diffusion coefficient and dSc denotes the sum of continuous drift/diffusion increments. The value of integrands at a finite number of dates does not alter those integrals. A pre-event stock holding Δu− earns Δu−J at the jump. Subtracting that gain leaves the exact gap

f(u,Su−+J)−f(u,Su−)−Δu−J.

Choosing Δ=fS cancels only the linear term. By the fundamental theorem of calculus twice, the residual is J²∫01(1−z)fSS(u,Su−+zJ)dz. For convex f it is nonnegative; for a short claim its sign in hedge wealth minus liability is negative. It equals ½ΓJ² exactly only for constant curvature along the jump segment. For a payoff kink the exact difference still makes sense, while a derivative approximation at the kink may not. A post-event hedge cannot retroactively earn the jump. Ex-dividend price jumps require adding the stock’s dividend cash to its total gain; do not mistake a known cash distribution for an uncompensated loss.

Worked example 3: the failure of a linear jump hedge

For f(S)=S²/100 and S−=100, the pre-event delta is 2. A fall by 20 changes the claim from 100 to 64, a loss of 36; two shares lose 40. The claim minus hedge change is +4=20²/100. A rise by 50 changes the claim by +125 while the hedge gains 100; the residual is +25. A delta-matched short claim loses 4 or 25 at the event, before any other carry or hedge error. A single share holding cannot match f over a continuum of jump sizes because that would require f(S+J) to be affine in J. For two possible outcomes and no other exposure, a secant hedge can span the outcomes as in Chapter 6; not every model with a jump is incomplete. The failure depends on the payoff span and instruments.

This theorem covers a finite specified event grid, sufficient for the lab’s contractual events. Unscheduled random jump times, compensators, Poisson changes of measure and infinite-activity processes require additional results. The pointwise pre-jump cash identity is still the relevant economic question, but no general Lévy pricing theorem has been established here.

6. Monitoring and history are part of the payoff

A terminal European call is (ST−K)+. A no-rebate, discretely monitored up-and-out call with observation set M pays (ST−K)+1{St<B for every t∈M}. Equality to B knocks it out under this contract. A sampled arithmetic Asian call with fixing set A pays (|A|−1Σt∈ASt−KA)+. These conventions exclude the initial mark unless it is expressly included. A different barrier direction, rebate, fixing weights, holiday rule or settlement date creates a different claim.

If M⊆M′ on the same probability space and the other terms agree, the up-and-out payoff on M′ is no greater path by path. Positive discounted expectation preserves this ordering, and stock/cash sub- and superhedge prices also preserve it because their constraints are ordered. This proof needs no Monte Carlo. It supplies no fixed rate at which a sequence of discrete monitoring values approaches a continuously monitored value. Jumps, discontinuous payoff rules and differing path models require separate analysis. An Asian average has no corresponding general monotonicity when a new fixing is added: that fixing may raise or lower the average.

Worked example 4: equal terminal prices, different path prices

The lab uses S0=100, D(2)=25/26, and the following original histories. The observations at .5 and 1.5 years locate credit events; exotic fixings and barrier observations are at years 1 and 2.

StateYear .5Year 1Year 1.5Year 2K=90 callB=130 up-outKA=100 Asian
Decline90807060000
Quiet recovery90809010010100
Spike and return11014012010010020
Advance11012013014050030

Two strictly positive pricing laws are pA=(.2,.4,.1,.3) and pB=(.2,.1,.4,.3). Both have E S2=104 and exactly the same terminal stock distribution. Therefore every payoff that is solely a function of S2, not just these calls, has the same price. The K=90 call costs (25/26)(20)=250/13≈19.230769 under either law. The up-out costs 50/13≈3.846154 under A and 25/26≈.961538 under B. The Asian costs 275/26≈10.576923 and 425/26≈16.346154. Terminal-only barrier monitoring would give payoff (0,10,10,0) and price 125/26≈4.807692 under both laws.

All positive laws satisfy p4−p1=.1. The closed extremes are (.45,0,0,.55), (0,.9,0,.1) and (0,0,.9,.1). Pair enumeration gives call bounds (175/13,1375/52), up-out bounds (0,225/26), and Asian bounds (75/26,525/26), all open. The stock is replicated, with the singleton price 100. Notice that the fine and coarse barriers have identical global bounds here even though their prices differ under A and B; an ordered pair of payoffs need not have strictly ordered extremal bounds.

Trading restriction matters. Intermediate values in this table are contractual marks, not stock quotes at which the lab permits transactions. Adding stock trading at those dates would impose conditional martingale restrictions and change the admissible laws and hedge span. The table proves lack of identification from the maturity-2 terminal distribution in its stated market; it does not prove that two dynamically traded diffusion models fit a full surface of all maturities. To compute a path-dependent claim on a richer finite tree, retain the running sum or barrier-alive indicator in the state and use the conditional laws at each node. Terminal-price recombination alone discards necessary history.

7. Credit derivatives: time every payment before pricing it

A reference default and the protection seller’s default are different events. Specify the reference entity, contractual trigger, notional N, premium dates tk, year fractions αk, default time τ, recovery fraction Rrec, and protection settlement time τ+ℓ. The following synthetic cash contract is an instructional definition, not a statement of current standard documentation: the protection buyer pays annual rate s until reference default, pays premium accrued since the preceding coupon at τ, and receives N(1−Rrec) at settlement. Reference default on a coupon date occurs before its scheduled coupon; the full elapsed coupon is instead included in accrued premium. Thus it is paid once. There is no premium after reference default. A historical treatment of premium, protection and accrued-premium distinctions is Duffie’s credit-swap article; current confirmations must be read directly for actual trades.

With deterministic discount factors D(t)>0 and a selected positive pricing law, define per-unit-notional annuity A and loss L:

A=EQ[ΣkD(tk)αk1{τ>tk}+D(τ)a(τ)1{τ≤T}],
L=EQ[D(τ+ℓ)(1−Rrec)1{τ≤T}],
Vbuyer=N(L−sA);   s*=L/A when A>0.

Here a(τ) is time since the last strictly earlier premium date under the declared day count, and τ=∞ on no-default paths. The formula follows by listing the cash at each date, discounting that date’s amount, and taking a finite-state expectation. It assumes no other cash flows and default-free counterparties. If A=0 and L>0, no finite running spread can finance the protection; if A=L=0 every rate gives zero value. A fixed coupon plus an upfront payment is a different quoting convention: the required buyer payment at inception is Vbuyer for the specified coupon, not a new premium rate.

To display seller exposure without claiming a general bilateral valuation formula, let the lab multiply protection by a state-specific paid fraction ζ∈[0,1]. Premium obligations of the default-free buyer are unchanged. Then replace the loss by ζ(1−Rrec). This is an expressly stipulated protection haircut contract; it does not model closeout, collateral, netting, replacement trades, buyer default or premium termination at seller failure. Those require additional cash-flow states and rules. Lower ζ precisely in severe reference-default states illustrates adverse dependence between the desired protection and the ability to collect it. Replacing the joint expectation by Eζ·E(1−Rrec) generally fails.

Worked example 5: default, accrued premium and delayed protection

Use the four-state histories and pA. Let D(.5)=100/101, D(1)=50/51, D(1.5)=100/103 and D(2)=25/26. Premium dates are years 1 and 2; N=100 and s=.03. In Decline, reference default occurs at .5, recovery is .25, the seller pays ζ=.5 of protection, and settlement is at year 1. The buyer pays 1.5 at .5 and receives 37.5 at 1: protection PV=625/17≈36.764706, premium PV=150/101≈1.485149. In Quiet recovery, reference default occurs at 1.5, recovery=.5, ζ=1, settlement=2; pay 3 at 1 and 1.5 at 1.5, receive 50 at 2. In the other two states there is no default and the buyer pays 3 at each annual date.

The unit annuity state values are (50/101, 7700/5253, 2575/1326, 2575/1326) years. Under A, protection PV is 5875/221≈26.583710; unit annuity A=10084475/6897189≈1.462113768 years; premium PV is 4.386341305; net buyer value is 3001950/135239≈22.197369. The zero-upfront running spread is 1466823/8067580≈.181816976 per year, or 1818.169761 basis points. These large numbers reflect intentionally severe synthetic default weights; they are not market observations.

Under B, protection PV falls to 12.160633484 and the annuity rises to 1.604944239; the fair spread is .075769819 per year. The laws fit the same terminal stock distribution but assign different credit weights. Recovery, default weights and counterparty paid fractions are separate inputs. Moving protection settlement to the actual default date changes its discount factor; it does not change premium accrual. If discount factors increase with time, a delay can increase PV, so no positive-rate conclusion should be silently imposed.

For the finite lab, a dated net cash vector Ci,k is equivalent at T to hi=ΣkD(tk)Ci,k/D(T), by bank borrowing or reinvestment. Its price is therefore D(T)Σpihi. The stock/cash bounds apply to this accumulated payoff, including negative premium obligations. For fair-spread bounds, write every p∈K as a convex combination Σwjvj of the listed laws. Since each law’s annuity Aj>0,

L(p)/A(p)=Σj[wjAj/ΣkwkAk]·[Lj/Aj].

Hence the extremal ratios occur among those laws. With the supplied inputs the spread set is (0,47277/165362), approximately (0,.285900025), with excluded endpoints. To justify exclusion when the ratio is nonconstant, at an extremal rate s the state vector Li−sAi has an extremal linear expectation of zero; our strict-positive endpoint argument applies. If all ratios agree, their common singleton is included. In a different contract zero-annuity boundary laws would require a separate analysis. The lab excludes them through positive default times and full accrued premium.

8. Reproduce, perturb and interpret the finite lab

Download the original inputs, standard-library model, exact output, SHA256 manifest and standalone instructions. From any directory run python3 v10-c11-analysis.py --input v10-c11-inputs.json --output result.json, adjusting paths as needed. No network, packages or random sample are required. Exact rational outputs are strings such as 25/26; they are not rounded decimal JSON numbers.

The implementation enumerates closed laws on one or two states and separately enumerates candidate sub- and superhedging lines. Saved output is not the sole oracle: the author checker reconstructs dated ledgers, checks independent rational grid and analytical cases, verifies invariances and boundary failures, and runs the model in isolation under normal and optimized Python. The declared finite domain is two to eight states and two to nine dates, bounded rational inputs and strictly interior forward. The README states all limits. The program rejects inconsistent pricing probabilities; it does not reinterpret them as estimates of P.

Useful interventions preserve one question at a time: exchange the two middle-state probabilities, remove a barrier observation, move protection settlement while preserving default time, alter the seller paid fraction in one default state, or change all discount factors while recalibrating pricing probabilities. Keep separate model-choice uncertainty, contractual monitoring, numerical approximation, sampling and arithmetic error. This lab has exact rational arithmetic and exhaustive finite enumeration. That eliminates rounding and simulation error inside its declared calculation, while leaving the adequacy of its states, trading restrictions and contract assumptions entirely open.

9. Exercises

  1. Replication and price range. In Worked example 1 replace the call by h=(0,10,30). Derive its price as a function of a, all no-arbitrage prices, and optimal affine sub- and superhedges. Demonstrate arbitrage at both endpoints.
  2. Proof: finite extremal laws. Explain why a linear expectation over K can attain its extrema on at most two states, including repeated x values. Prove why the average of all such feasible extremal laws is strictly positive when min x<F<max x. Identify what fails if F=max x while a smaller x state has positive P.
  3. Another instrument. In the three-state market a digital d=(0,1,0) is traded at price 25/52. Find the resulting pricing probabilities and the price of h=(0,0,40). Replicate that call using stock, terminal cash and the digital. Explain why the digital’s own zero or 25/26 price is inadmissible.
  4. Proof: independent-driver calculus. Derive the weighted cross-variation L² bound for bounded left-endpoint-adapted H. For X=W1 and Y=ρW1+√(1−ρ²)W2, use the proved vector formula on f(x,y)=xy. Identify the drift and verify E[XtYt].
  5. Local hedge transfer. Repeat Worked example 2 with VY=−8, leaving other inputs unchanged. Find the minimum instantaneous-variance stock holding and its residual variance. With the same G, find the two-instrument hedge. Explain the conditions under which that calculation fails to establish a global replication.
  6. Proof: a remaining risk premium. For the bounded-volatility construction in Section 4, explain why tilting W2 leaves the traded stock a true martingale. At T=4 compare the digital prices for λ=0 and λ=1/2. Would a normalizing positive density alone prove the stock’s martingale property in an unbounded-volatility model?
  7. Finite jump accounting. Let f(S)=S³/10000 at S−=100. Compute its delta and the exact claim-minus-delta-hedge residual for J=−20 and J=50. Compare with ½f″(100)J². Derive the finite-event-date formula’s jump contribution and explain the error in using a post-jump delta.
  8. History and monitoring. For the four histories in Worked example 4, lower the barrier to 120, retaining observations at years 1 and 2. Calculate the payoff and prices under A and B. Then monitor only at T and calculate again. State and prove the monitoring ordering, and explain why adding Asian fixings has no analogous universal ordering.
  9. Credit cash timing. In Worked example 5, move protection settlement to reference default, leaving every other rule unchanged. Recompute protection PV, net value and fair spread under A. Then restore delayed settlement and set ζ=1 in Decline. Calculate the increments in protection PV and fair spread. Explain why multiplying independent averages is not an adequate replacement for the state ledger.
  10. Proof: ratio bounds and a boundary. Prove the extremal-law formula for fair-spread bounds when all annuities are positive. In a two-state toy contract with L=(1,0), A=(0,1), what happens to L(p)/A(p) as p1→1? Explain why our finite ratio bound must not be used without checking denominators.
  11. Physical law, admissibility and changing the market. A researcher assigns physical probabilities (.2,.4,.1,.3) to the four histories and therefore calls them the uniquely correct pricing probabilities. A second researcher introduces stock trading at year 1 while keeping the same two pricing laws. Diagnose both arguments. Give a numerical conditional-martingale failure under law A using the year-1 mark 140.
  12. Model and research critique. Assess this memo: “Our vanilla fit proves the exotic price; two factors always imply incompleteness; one extra option always restores completeness; jumps are covered by vega; CDS spread divided by loss given default is the physical hazard; a narrower Monte Carlo interval resolves the disputed protection-settlement date.” Replace each assertion with a defensible, testable statement and design one identification test, one contractual test and one implementation test. State what each test cannot establish.
Complete solutions and assessment criteria

  1. Eph=10(.9−2a)+30(.1+a)=12+10a, so c∈(150/13,825/52), approximately (11.538462,15.865385). The subhedge .5x−40 pays (−10,10,30), costs 150/13. The superhedge .375x−22.5 pays (0,15,30), costs 825/52. Their bounds equal the limits at a=0 and .45, so they are optimal. Buying the claim and shorting the subhedge at the lower endpoint pays (10,0,0); buying the superhedge and shorting the claim at the upper endpoint pays (0,5,0). Both cost zero and have positive P-probability of profit. Unequal successive slopes .25 and .5 exclude replication.

  2. On support size ≥3 the two equations Σz=Σzx=0 have a nonzero solution. At an extremum, an improving direction is impossible, so Σzh=0; move to a first vanishing coordinate without changing the objective, then repeat. A pair of distinct outcomes bracketing F has the unique nonnegative weights in Section 2; equal outcomes allow a feasible singleton only at F. Each state belongs with positive weight to one feasible listed law: pair it with an opposite-side outcome or use its singleton. Their finite equal-weight average is therefore positive everywhere. If F=max x, Epx=F forces p to vanish on every smaller outcome; no equivalent positive law exists. Directly, buying the bank terminal amount max x and shorting the stock costs D max x−S0=0 and pays max x−x, strictly positive in that smaller state. The interior hypothesis prevents this arbitrage.

  3. The digital price gives p2=(25/52)/(25/26)=1/2, so a=1/5 and p=(1/5,1/2,3/10). The call price is 150/13. Match the two extreme states with .5 shares and A=−30; their payoff vector is (0,20,40). Short 20 digitals to get (0,0,40). Cost 50−30(25/26)−20(25/52)=150/13. All three state vectors are now linearly spanned. A zero digital quote gives a free nonnegative claim positive in the middle state; quote D=25/26 lets one buy terminal cash 1 and short the digital at zero cost, paying (1,0,1). The stock calibration tightens the actual digital price interval to (0,(9/10)D)=(0,45/52), since p₂=.9−2a with 0<a<.45. At the true upper endpoint 45/52, buy the superhedge (140−x)/40, whose payoff is (2,1,0), and short the digital: its cost is (25/26)(7/2)−100/40=45/52 and the combined payoff is (2,0,0). Thus that endpoint also gives a zero-cost arbitrage. The requested quote D lies even above this bound.

  4. Set Zi=HiΔW1,iΔW2,i. Conditional on the left endpoint, E Zi=0 and E Zi²=E Hi²(Δti)². For i<j, ZiHj is past-measurable at tj, so E ZiZj=0. Thus E(ΣZ)2≤||H||²∞t·mesh. For f=xy, fx=y, fy=x, fxy=fyx=1 and other second derivatives zero. Hence d(XY)=YdW1+X[ρdW1+√(1−ρ²)dW2]+ρdt. The stochastic terms have zero expectation since ∫E(X²+Y²)dt<∞, so E XtYt=ρt, agreeing with the Gaussian covariance.

  5. The first coefficient is 20(.55)−.18(−8)=12.44. The stock holding is .622; the remaining coefficient is .24(−8)=−1.92, and residual variance is 3.6864dt. With GY=6, η=−4/3 and Δ=.55−(−4/3)(.25)=53/60≈.883333. Check both drivers: the Y coefficient is matched because ηGY=−8, and the S partial because Δ+η(.25)=.55. Values and bank cash must still be financed. Rank can fail if GY, β or √(1−ρ²) vanishes; integrability, terminal matching, trading permissions, costs and solvency are not supplied by a pointwise linear system. A vanishing determinant is a warning, not proof that every claim becomes unhedgeable.

  6. The joint normal density factors, so Qλ changes only W2 into B2−λt, leaving W1 Brownian independent of B2. The stock differential keeps zero drift; bounded σ gives E S²≤S0²e.25²t by stopped Itô and the integral inequality, then finite E∫σ²S²dt makes its integral a true L² martingale. At T=4, prices are Φ(0)=.5 and Φ(−1)≈.158655254. A normalizing density proves a probability law, not integrability or preservation of a given local martingale’s expectation. Unbounded coefficients require new conditions and an actual martingale argument. Our result does not authorize arbitrary stochastic factor-drift changes.

  7. f(100)=100, f′(100)=3 and f″(100)=.06. Expanding the cubic gives residual (3·100·J²+J³)/10000=.03J²+J³/10000. For J=−20 this is 12−.8=11.2: f(80)−f(100)=−48.8 while the hedge loses 60. For J=50 it is 75+12.5=87.5: f(150)−f(100)=237.5 while the hedge gains 150. The constant-gamma approximation gives 12 and 75 and omits the cubic remainder. Summing exact changes at each event date after applying continuous Itô on intervening intervals produces Σ[f(u,Su)−f(u,Su−)]. Stock gains use holdings decided before the move, so a post-jump delta is not the holding that earned J; using it introduces hindsight and generally gives a different, unfunded gain.

  8. At B=120, equality knocks out Advance already at year 1; Spike also knocks out. Decline’s call is zero and Quiet survives. The fine-grid payoff remains (0,10,0,0), prices 50/13 and 25/26. With only terminal observation, Quiet and Spike both survive, giving (0,10,10,0), price 125/26 under either law. Enlarging M shrinks the event “all observations below B”; multiplication by a nonnegative call and positive expectation proves the ordering under a common law. A prior Asian average of 100 becomes 110 if a new equally weighted observation of 120 is added to a single fixing, or 90 if that observation is 80. A call strike of 95 then respectively rises from 5 to 15 or falls to zero. Changing the model law at the same time would invalidate the pure monitoring comparison.

  9. Immediate protection PV under A is (.2)(37.5)(100/101)+(.4)(50)(100/103)=750/101+2000/103≈26.843218302. The annuity stays 1.4621137683772332, so net value is approximately 22.456876997 and fair spread is approximately .183591858. With delayed settlement restored and ζ raised from .5 to 1 in Decline, the additional state protection is 37.5 paid at year 1. Its expected PV increment is (.2)(37.5)(50/51)=125/17≈7.352941176. The fair-spread increment is that number divided by 100A, approximately .050289802 per year. The joint state ledger knows which default is severe, which recovery applies, which seller fraction is paid and when. A product of marginal averages would be justified only by suitable independence, including the relevant timing and default indicator, none of which this construction supplies. Full precision checks are in the lab checker; these figures are rounded teaching displays.

  10. If p=Σwjvj with w≥0 and Σw=1, linearity gives L(p)=ΣwLj and A(p)=ΣwAj. Divide by the positive denominator and rewrite the ratio as a weighted mean of Lj/Aj, using weights wjAj/ΣwA. It lies between the smallest and largest listed ratios, both reached on the closed set. A nonconstant ratio cannot reach either at a strictly positive law by applying the endpoint proof to L−sA. For the toy contract put p1=p, p2=1−p. The ratio p/(1−p) diverges to +∞ as p→1. At the endpoint A=0,L=1 there is no finite spread. A program returning a finite upper bound by discarding that zero denominator would be wrong.

  11. The first vector happens to be stock-calibrated, so it is one valid Q. No-arbitrage does not identify it as unique: the second positive vector (.2,.1,.4,.3) also prices stock and bank. Physical estimation supplies frequencies and perhaps a preference-based risk-premium model; frequencies alone do not eliminate the other measures. The new trading date changes the attainable set. At year 1, mark 140 uniquely identifies Spike in the table, whose terminal stock is surely 100. Under A the conditional discounted terminal value at that node is [D(2)/D(1)]100=(51/52)100≈98.076923, not 140. Thus A does not price a tradable year-1 stock at that mark; neither does B. Selling it at 140 and buying bank cash sufficient for 100 at year 2 would generate a sure surplus at that reached node. Conditional calibration and trading rules must be rebuilt before applying a dynamic theorem.

  12. Illustrative answer. A vanilla fit tests selected marginal-payoff prices within a family; compare path-dependent prices under distinct laws that fit those quotes. Factor labels do not determine rank: check independent random exposures and their coefficients, including β=0 and |ρ|=1. An extra option helps only where its factor exposure gives an invertible matrix, and global funding, regularity and admissibility still need proof. Vega measures sensitivity to a specified parameter; a finite jump produces an exact payoff gap that is not erased by a generic vega hedge. A spread is a cash-flow valuation under pricing weights, recoveries and payment timing; a physical hazard requires separate statistical and premium assumptions. More simulation resolves sampling noise, not missing contract terms.

    An identification test can hold all terminal prices fixed while shifting Quiet/Spike mass, then compare barrier and credit values; it reveals nonidentification in that market but not which law describes reality. A contractual test enumerates default exactly on coupon dates, barrier equality and settlement delay; it checks the specified logic but cannot certify legal enforceability. An implementation test compares rational hedge costs with independently computed extremal expectations and reconstructs dated cash flows; it catches arithmetic/logic failures but does not validate the state model. Rubric, 12 points: one for each of six corrected assertions; one for each of three concrete tests; one for each correctly stated test limitation. An answer that treats a confidence interval as identification evidence or omits counterparty cash rules must be revised.

10. Teach-back and delayed retention

Teach-back prompt. Explain to a colleague how a model can be free of arbitrage yet leave a derivative’s price uncertain. Use one finite portfolio calculation and one cash-flow example; distinguish changing a pricing law from making a numerical calculation more accurate.

Model response. In the three-state market, stock and bank span only affine functions of terminal stock. Positive pricing laws indexed by a all price those assets correctly, while the call costs (25/26)(4+40a). Sub- and superhedges give a strict interval; at its endpoints a residual positive payoff is free. Selecting a law inside it is an additional modeling decision. In the credit example, default at .5 creates an accrued premium at .5 and delayed protection at 1; moving protection to .5 changes the contract PV under the same law. Exact rational arithmetic can check either calculation, but it cannot choose a missing risk premium or settle an unspecified payment date.

Retention check, after one week without notes. (1) What is the price set of a replicated affine payoff? (2) With β=.4, ρ=0 and VY=5, what residual instantaneous variance remains after matching the stock driver? (3) For f=S²/100 and J=−30, what is claim minus delta-hedge change? (4) Is a barrier observation at exact equality B safe under this chapter’s contract? (5) If a selected credit law gives unit loss PV .06 and annuity 1.5 years, what is the fair running spread?

Answers. (1) The singleton containing its stock/cash cost, including that endpoint. (2) (.4·5)²dt=4dt. (3) J²/100=9, assuming the post-jump stock remains in domain. (4) No: equality knocks out. (5) .06/1.5=.04 per year, 400 basis points, under that pricing law and cash schedule. Revisit Sections 1–2 for pricing versus forecasting, Sections 3–5 for exposure and jumps, and Sections 6–7 for contractual mistakes.

Further study and boundary of this chapter. The finite bounds and conditional claims here are original derivations; the finite-market notes, continuous-model extensions, and historical credit-swap study locate the wider literature. General semimartingale asset pricing, stochastic factor-risk-premium measure changes, Heston/CIR boundary theory, random-time jump compensators, calibration identification and bilateral collateralized credit valuation require additional hypotheses and proofs. No source’s broader theorem or historical trading convention has been substituted for those missing steps. Chapter 12 turns these distinctions into reproducible model-use and validation decisions.

Sources and further study

  • Martin Haugh — Martingale Pricing Theory in Discrete-Time and Discrete-Space Models (2016), single-period completeness sections — Further reading for positive state prices, attainability, finite-market completeness and nonunique pricing measures. The chapter supplies its own constructive stock/cash envelope proof, endpoint qualification, original states and exercises, without invoking the source's linear-programming duality route.
  • Martin Haugh — Local Volatility, Stochastic Volatility and Jump-Diffusion Models (Fall 2013) — Further-study map for volatility-factor exposure, missing hedging instruments and jump payoff changes. Original bounded-factor constant-tilt example, restricted independent-driver proof and deterministic finite-event telescoping proof establish only the results used in the chapter.
  • Darrell Duffie — Credit Swap Valuation, Financial Analysts Journal 55(1), 73–87 (January/February 1999) — Historical primary exposition of premium versus protection cash flows, accrued-premium and settlement-date distinctions, and the need to state counterparty assumptions. All finite-state credit contracts, numbers and fair-spread ratio proofs in this chapter are original instructional constructions.
